extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in hoaxes, misinformation, and media history
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview that defines what a hoax is, distinguishes it from related phenomena (rumour, prank, fraud, magic), describes motives, mechanisms, types, notable examples, and features of hoax news and successful hoaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a hoax
rubrics_metrics.description: A hoax (pl.: hoaxes) is a widely publicised falsehood created to deceive its audience with false and often astonishing information, with either malicious or humorous intent of causing shock and interest in as many people as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the audience being unaware of the deception; some hoaxers later unmask their work to expose victims as fools, while others maintain the deception indefinitely. Examples and historical context (e.g., the Dihydrogen monoxide hoax, Jonathan Swift's almanac) illustrate that hoaxes may be constructed using true statements in misleading contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hoax versus urban legend/rumour
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction: the term 'hoax' should be used only for those cases with a probable conscious attempt to deceive, whereas many urban legends and rumours lack evidence of deliberate creation and are passed along in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on folklorist Jan Harold Brunvand's view: use 'hoax' when there is evidence of intentional fabrication; otherwise prefer 'urban legend' or 'rumour'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hoax versus practical joke/prank
rubrics_metrics.description: A hoax tends to indicate 'relatively complex and large-scale fabrications' and includes deceptions that go beyond the merely playful and 'cause material loss or harm to the victim', unlike practical jokes or pranks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlap exists in some cases, but hoaxes are generally larger in scale and can have serious consequences; use this distinction when categorising an incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motives and goals of hoaxers
rubrics_metrics.description: Hoaxers may be motivated by varied goals: to embarrass, to provoke social or political change, to gain monetary profit or fame, to ridicule opponents, to market products or media, or to expose victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: P. T. Barnum's Fiji mermaid (monetary/fame), political hoaxes timed before elections (ridicule/undermine opponents), marketing-staged incidents for film promotion (e.g., staged 'wedding' video). Distinction between hoax and fraud is sometimes blurred; Alex Boese notes the public's reaction can determine classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channels and mechanics of hoax propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hoaxes can be communicated by any means a fictional story can be communicated: in person, word of mouth, printed material, chain letters, newspapers, tabloids, and increasingly via social networking websites and fake news websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technological developments (printing press, rotary press, email, social media) change the speed and scale of spread. Recognize that the medium affects reach and entrenchment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of hoax news (fake news)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hoax news is a news report containing facts that are inaccurate or false but which are presented as genuine; it often conveys a half-truth used deliberately to mislead the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoax news commonly uses sensationalist or deceptive headlines to maximise readership and may be used for financial or political gain; unlike news satire, fake-news sites seek to mislead rather than entertain. Hoax news can serve propaganda or disinformation campaigns and may be amplified via social media to drive web traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peter Hancock's six steps for a successful hoax
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychologist Peter Hancock identified six steps which characterise a truly successful hoax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The six steps are: (1) Identify a constituency (a group who will care about the creation); (2) Identify a particular dream which will make your hoax appeal to that constituency; (3) Create an appealing but 'under-specified' hoax, with ambiguities; (4) Have your creation discovered; (5) Find at least one champion who will actively support your hoax; (6) Make people care, either positively or negatively — the ambiguities encourage interest and debate. These are presented as design principles for crafting hoaxes that gain traction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical patterns of computer-virus hoaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: A common hoax type is the computer-virus hoax: email warnings about non-existent threats, often forging quotes from authorities and exhorting recipients to distribute the message (the 'virus' is the message itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some virus-hoax messages become harmful by instructing users to delete critical system files or to take damaging actions; recognize signs such as broad distribution requests, unverifiable authority quotes, and instructions that would impair normal functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and categories of hoaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hoaxes occur in many domains: academic hoaxes (e.g., Sokal affair), art-world hoaxes, paleoanthropological hoaxes (e.g., Piltdown Man), protest hoaxes, religious hoaxes, UFO hoaxes, 'hoax of exposure' (sting operations), and others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists many exemplars and subtypes; when analysing or classifying an incident, map it to the most appropriate category and consider domain-specific consequences and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scare-tactic hoaxes and cost-asymmetry exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some hoaxes use scare tactics that appeal to an audience's subjective calculation that the expected cost of not believing (if true) outweighs the cost of believing (if false), e.g., false malware warnings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These hoaxes exploit risk perception and encourage precautionary or panic responses; identifying and countering them requires addressing the perceived cost asymmetry and providing verifiable authoritative information.

rubrics_metrics.name: State and propaganda-related hoaxes (black propaganda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments sometimes spread false information, sometimes mixing outright hoax with suppression and information management to give a desired impression, often to facilitate objectives such as going to war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include spoof broadcasts or false invasion reports; treat such cases as potentially coordinated disinformation campaigns with political objectives and possible use of censorship/suppression to shape public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and criminal consequences of hoaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal hoax admissions can divert police investigations and have legal consequences; perpetrators can be charged under offences such as perverting the course of justice and wasting police time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the 'Wearside Jack' case. When evaluating the impact of a hoax, consider potential legal liability and the diversion of public resources as part of its harm profile.
